title-group.article-title: Aβ₁₋₄₀ Enhances Platelet Sensitivity to Thrombin via NADPH Oxidase–ROS Signaling and Integrin αIIbβ3 Engagement

abstract.p: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder with significant vascular involvement, with microvascular damage and thromboinflammation often preceding classical amyloid pathology by several years. Elevated levels of prothrombin and thrombin, along with aberrant platelet activation, have been reported in individuals with AD. We hypothesized that platelet hyperactivity in AD results from an exaggerated response to thrombin in the presence of elevated amyloid beta 1-40 (Aβ₁₋₄₀), a peptide that accumulates during the early stages of AD. Platelet activation in response to Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin was assessed using aggregation assays with an aggregometer, adhesion measurements by confocal microscopy, and spreading via both confocal microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and integrin αIIbβ3 activation were quantified by flow cytometry. The roles of NADPH oxidase (NOX), ROS, and integrin signaling were examined using selective inhibitors. Aβ₁₋₄₀ significantly enhanced thrombin-induced platelet adhesion, aggregation, and spreading via NOX-derived ROS and integrin αIIbβ3 activation. Aβ₁₋₄₀ also promoted platelet binding to fibrinogen and cerebrovascular endothelial cells, accompanied by distinct morphological changes. Inhibition of NOX or integrin αIIbβ3 significantly reduced these effects. These findings identify a novel Aβ₁₋₄₀–NOX–ROS–integrin αIIbβ3 axis that drives platelet hyperactivation and cerebrovascular interactions in AD. Targeting this pathway with antithrombotic or antioxidative strategies may offer therapeutic potential in mitigating AD-associated vascular pathology.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder primarily characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide accumulation, neurofibrillary tangles, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline (Busche and Hyman, 2020). While the central nervous system has traditionally been the focus of AD pathogenesis, increasing evidence points to significant cerebrovascular and systemic vascular dysfunction in AD patients (Strickland, 2018). In particular, Aβ₁₋₄₀, the predominant isoform circulating in the bloodstream and deposited along cerebral vessel walls, has been linked to vascular inflammation, endothelial injury, and heightened thrombogenicity (Herzig et al., 2004). Clinical observations of microvascular thrombosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), and elevated stroke incidence among patients with AD support the concept of “vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID),” in which amyloid peptides exacerbate cerebrovascular pathology.

A critical mediator of this vascular component is platelet activation (Zhang et al., 2013). Beyond their established roles in thrombosis and hemostasis, platelets actively participate in neuroinflammation and vascular endothelial interactions. Numerous studies have shown that Aβ₁₋₄₀ can induce platelet aggregation, upregulate procoagulant surface markers, and modulate platelet–endothelium adhesion. Mechanistically, Aβ₁₋₄₀ stimulates the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including superoxide (O₂⁻) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), primarily through activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) (Donner et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2021). Among the NOX isoforms, NOX2 is abundantly expressed in platelets and constitutes a principal source of oxidative signaling during platelet activation. Dysregulated NOX activity has been associated with enhanced platelet reactivity, prothrombotic states, and vascular damage in various pathological contexts, including atherosclerosis, diabetes, ischemic stroke, and neurodegenerative diseases. ROS contribute to the activation of integrin αIIbβ3, a critical receptor complex responsible for fibrinogen binding, platelet aggregation, and thrombus stabilization (Donner et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2021). Under physiological conditions, integrin activation proceeds through a tightly regulated inside-out signaling cascade. However, oxidative stress and inflammation can lead to aberrant integrin activation, increasing platelet adhesion to extracellular matrix proteins and vascular endothelial surfaces. Both Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin have independently been shown to stimulate NOX-mediated ROS production and upregulate integrin αIIbβ3 on platelets, suggesting the potential for convergent signaling that amplifies platelet activation and vascular adhesion.

Thrombin, a serine protease generated during the coagulation cascade, is among the most potent endogenous platelet activators. Acting via protease-activated receptors (PARs), thrombin initiates rapid integrin activation, cytoskeletal remodeling, and granule secretion. Elevated thrombin levels have been documented in conditions involving neuroinflammation, traumatic brain injury, and AD. Importantly, platelets from patients with AD demonstrate heightened responsiveness to thrombin, potentially reflecting a primed phenotype resulting from chronic exposure to circulating Aβ and oxidative stressors (Grammas et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2005; Zipser et al., 2007). Despite these observations, the extent of the enhanced response involving Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin, as well as the specific molecular pathways of their interaction, remains poorly understood. Most prior studies have examined Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin in isolation, with few addressing their combined or sequential effects on shared NOX–ROS–integrin pathways. Moreover, it is unclear whether such interactions culminate in morphological changes or increased platelet adhesion to cerebrovascular endothelial cells, both of which are relevant to thromboinflammatory processes in AD.

To address these gaps, we investigated whether Aβ₁₋₄₀ amplifies thrombin-induced platelet activation and explored the underlying molecular mechanisms. Specifically, we examined the roles of NOX-derived ROS and integrin αIIbβ3 activation using selective pharmacological inhibitors. We further evaluated downstream functional consequences, including cytoskeletal remodeling and adhesion to human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMECs). Through this mechanistic framework, we aim to elucidate how amyloid and coagulation pathways intersect to drive cerebrovascular inflammation in AD.

sec.title: Reagents
sec.p: Aβ₁₋₄₀ (human) was purchased from Abcam (San Francisco, CA, USA), and PLCγ2 antibody was obtained from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX, USA). VAS2870 was purchased from Enzo Life Sciences (Farmingdale, NY, USA), and Trolox from Tocris Bioscience (Ellisville, MO, USA). Eptifibatide was purchased from Millipore (Burlington, MA, USA). FITC-conjugated anti-human CD41a (integrin αIIb) and APC-conjugated anti-human CD61 (integrin β3) antibodies were purchased from BD Pharmingen (San Diego, CA, USA). CellTracker™ Green 5-chloromethylfluorescein diacetate (CMFDA), FITC-labeled 2’,7’-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H2DCFDA), and PE/Cy5-labeled dihydroethidium (DHE) were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA).

sec.title: Preparation of washed platelets
sec.p: Human whole blood was collected from healthy volunteers following ethical approval by the Ajou University Ethics Committee (202211-HM-EX-001). Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) samples were also obtained from healthy donors through the Korean Red Cross Center. PRP was centrifuged at 1,000×g for 10 min at 23°C, avoiding disruption of the platelet pellet. The resulting pellet was washed twice with Tyrode buffer (pH 7.4) and resuspended to a final concentration of 2×10⁸ cells/mL for use in optical aggregometry, flow cytometry, ROS assays, immunoblotting, and adhesion studies.

sec.title: Platelet aggregation
sec.p: Light transmission aggregometry was performed using a Chronolog aggregometer (Chrono-Log Corporation). PRP samples were preincubated with or without Aβ₁₋₄₀ for 5 min, followed by stimulation with thrombin at concentrations of 0.03, 0.05, 0.075, and 0.1 U/mL. Platelets were pretreated with Aβ₁₋₄₀ (0.1, 1, or 10 μg/mL), trolox (100 μM), VAS2870 (10 μM), or eptifibatide (50 μM) for 5 min before agonist addition. Aggregation was recorded at 37°C for 6 min. Additional measurements were performed using a 490D coagulometer (Chrono-Log Corporation) for 5 min at 37°C. Maximum aggregation within 8 min post-stimulation was recorded as mean ± SEM. The EC₅₀ was calculated from dose-response curves for each donor, and average EC₅₀ values were determined across donors.

sec.title: Platelet adhesion to fibrinogen
sec.p: Glass-bottom dishes were coated with fibrinogen (10 μg/mL) at 37°C for 30 min. Following washing with BSA-containing buffer, CMFDA-labeled platelets (10 μM) were incubated on the coated surface at 37°C for 30 min. Non-adherent cells were removed by gentle washing with PBS. Images from randomly selected fields were acquired using a confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan). Adhesion was quantified by calculating the area occupied by adherent platelets as a percentage of the total imaged area. Experiments were repeated independently three to five times.

sec.title: Measurement of filopodia length in platelet
sec.p: Filopodia length on immobilized fibrinogen was assessed using confocal microscopy (Nikon, Japan). Platelet images were captured at 600× magnification. Membrane protrusions (filopodia) were analyzed from 20 randomly selected fields using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA) to determine platelet surface area and filopodia extension.

sec.title: Analysis of integrin αIIb and β3 activation by flow cytometry
sec.p: Washed platelets (2×10⁸/mL) were activated with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin, then washed with Tyrode buffer and fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde on ice for 20 min. Platelets were stained with FITC-conjugated anti-human CD41a (integrin αIIb) and APC-conjugated anti-human CD61 (integrin β3) antibodies for 20 min at 4°C. After washing, samples were analyzed using a FACS Aria III flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA).

sec.title: Measurement of NADPH oxidase activity
sec.p: NOX activity in intact platelets was measured using a lucigenin-enhanced chemiluminescence assay (Hur et al., 2025). Lucigenin reacts with superoxide anions to produce luminescence, which was quantified using a luminometer. The reaction mixture contained 1 mM EGTA and 5 μM lucigenin in phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). The reaction was initiated by adding 50 μM NADPH immediately prior to measurement. Luminescence was detected using a tabletop luminometer (BD Systems), and values were averaged per sample.

sec.title: Measurement of ROS
sec.p: Intracellular ROS production was evaluated using a single-cell fluorescence assay with H₂DCFDA and DHE (Ji et al., 2021). H₂DCFDA is oxidized to fluorescent 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein (DCF) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻), hydroperoxides, and hydroxyl radicals (•OH). DHE is oxidized to fluorescent ethidium upon interaction with superoxide (O₂⁻). Platelets treated with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin were incubated with 10 μM H₂DCFDA or 10 μM DHE for 30 min. Fluorescence was measured using a FACSAria III flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA). All measurements were performed in five independent experiments.

sec.title: Primary hBMEC culture
sec.p: Primary hBMECs (ACBRI 376) were purchased from Cell Systems (Seattle, WA, USA) and cultured per the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were maintained in Complete Classic Medium with serum and CultureBoost™ (Cat. 4Z0-500) at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO₂. Cells were seeded in T-flasks and subcultured prior to reaching 80% confluence. Media were replaced every 2 days. Only cells at passages 5 or 6 were used to ensure phenotypic consistency. For platelet adhesion assays, cells were plated on Attachment Factor™ (Cat. 4ZO-210)-coated coverslips or culture dishes and allowed to reach 70–80% confluence prior to experimentation.

sec.title: Platelet adhesion to hBMEC
sec.p: Washed platelets were seeded onto glass-bottom dishes pre-cultured with hBMECs (2×10⁵ cells/dish) and incubated at 37°C for 1 h. After incubation, cells were fixed with 1% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100, and rinsed with PBS containing 1% BSA. Platelets were stained with anti-CD41a antibody (1:100, EPR4330, Abcam) overnight at 37°C. Nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst. Adherent platelets were visualized in five randomly selected fields per dish using a confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan). Quantification was performed using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA).

sec.title: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
sec.p: Platelets were allowed to adhere to fibrinogen-coated coverslips for 30 min. Samples were fixed in a solution containing 2.5% glutaraldehyde, 4% paraformaldehyde, 0.2 M sucrose, and 0.1 M sodium cacodylate (pH 7.4) for 30 min at room temperature. After fixation, samples were mounted, dehydrated, and air-dried. Imaging was performed using a field-emission scanning electron microscope.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 (GraphPad Software, Inc. San Diego, CA, USA). For comparisons among more than two groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was used. For comparisons between two groups, unpaired two-tailed t-tests were performed.

sec.title: Aβ₁₋₄₀ potentiates thrombin-induced platelet activation
sec.p: The experimental design and time-dependent analyses are summarized in Fig. 1A. To determine whether Aβ₁₋₄₀ modulates thrombin-induced platelet adhesion, we examined the adherence of human platelets to fibrinogen-coated surfaces. Both Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin individually increased platelet adhesion in a concentration-dependent manner. Aβ₁₋₄₀ increased adhesion to 120.8 ± 6.4% at 0.1 μM and to 318.1 ± 28.1% at 10 μM, while thrombin increased adhesion to 193.6 ± 20.9% at 0.05 U/mL and to 390.3 ± 31.0% at 0.1 U/mL. Notably, pretreatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ (0.1 μM) significantly enhanced thrombin (0.05 U/mL)-induced adhesion to fibrinogen to 398.2 ± 20.9%, exceeding the response induced by either stimulus alone (Fig. 1B). We next evaluated whether Aβ₁₋₄₀ similarly modulates thrombin-induced platelet aggregation. While Aβ₁₋₄₀ alone did not elicit substantial aggregation, pretreatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ markedly augmented thrombin-induced aggregation in a concentration-dependent manner. Co-treatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ (0.1 μM) and thrombin (0.05 U/mL) resulted in 70.3 ± 2.4% aggregation, which was comparable to that induced by 0.1 U/mL thrombin (76.2 ± 4.5%), a physiologically robust stimulus (Fig. 1C). These results indicate that Aβ₁₋₄₀ primes platelets to respond more strongly to subthreshold thrombin stimulation, thereby enhancing platelet activation.

sec.title: Integrin αIIbβ3 Is involved in Aβ₁₋₄₀–mediated enhancement of platelet activation
sec.p: Given that platelet adhesion and aggregation are critically dependent on integrin αIIbβ3 (Zou et al., 2022), we investigated whether the Aβ₁₋₄₀–mediated enhancement of thrombin-induced activation requires integrin αIIbβ3 signaling. Platelet adhesion and aggregation assays were performed in the presence or absence of the integrin αIIbβ3 inhibitor eptifibatide (eptif). Fluorescence imaging showed that co-treatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin increased platelet adhesion to 398.2 ± 19.4% relative to control, whereas pretreatment with eptifibatide (50 μM) significantly reduced adhesion to 150.5 ± 12.3% (Fig. 2A). Platelets adhered to fibrinogen typically exhibit membrane spreading and filopodia formation (Bender and Palankar, 2021). DIC microscopy revealed pronounced filopodia extension and spreading in platelets treated with Aβ₁₋₄₀ + thrombin, which were markedly attenuated by eptifibatide pretreatment (Fig. 2B). In aggregation assays, Aβ₁₋₄₀ + thrombin induced 70.3 ± 2.4% aggregation, compared with 47.8 ± 4.2% with thrombin alone. This potentiation was almost completely abolished by eptifibatide, reducing aggregation to 3.5 ± 1.4% (Fig. 2C). Together, these findings indicate that Aβ₁₋₄₀ amplifies platelet activation through integrin αIIbβ3-dependent mechanisms.

sec.title: Aβ₁₋₄₀ enhances ROS generation and integrin αIIbβ3 signaling in thrombin-activated platelets
sec.p: We investigated whether the enhanced platelet adhesion and aggregation observed with integrin αIIbβ3 activation are associated with oxidative stress. Aβ₁₋₄₀ alone did not significantly increase ROS production (O₂⁻ or H₂O₂) compared with untreated controls. Thrombin stimulation induced a moderate rise in O₂⁻ levels; however, co-treatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin markedly increased both O₂⁻ and H₂O₂ production (464.9 ± 48.3% and 239.9 ± 27.8%, respectively). These elevations were significantly reduced by the antioxidant Trolox (to 242.9 ± 44.4% and 115.0 ± 6.4%, respectively; Fig. 3A, 3B), indicating that Aβ₁₋₄₀ amplifies thrombin-induced ROS generation. To determine whether ROS influenced integrin αIIbβ3 signaling, we examined the activation of integrin αIIb and β3 following stimulation with Aβ₁₋₄₀ in the presence or absence of Trolox. Thrombin significantly increased integrin αIIb and β3 activation, consistent with the observed ROS production. Pretreatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ further enhanced thrombin-induced integrin activation (303.1 ± 20.9% and 315.3 ± 24.8%, respectively), whereas co-treatment with Trolox attenuated these effects (153.8 ± 33.0% and 185.8 ± 36.3%; Fig. 3C, 3D). In addition, Trolox markedly reduced platelet adhesion (from 452.2 ± 13.2% to 193.6 ± 28.3%) and aggregation (from 70.3 ± 2.4% to 25.7 ± 3.7%; Fig. 3E, 3F). These findings indicate that ROS generation is a key mediator of Aβ₁₋₄₀-induced platelet activation through upregulation of integrin αIIbβ3 signaling.

sec.title: NOX mediates integrin αIIbβ3-dependent ROS production in platelets
sec.p: Given that ROS production in platelets is largely NOX-dependent (Violi and Pignatelli, 2014), we next investigated whether NOX contributes to Aβ₁₋₄₀– and thrombin-induced ROS generation and integrin αIIbβ3 activation. Time-course analysis revealed that NOX activity progressively increased following co-treatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin, peaking at 5 min (564.3 ± 51.5%) compared with thrombin alone (290.0 ± 59.4%). This increase was significantly inhibited by the NOX inhibitor VAS2870 (10 μM), which reduced activity to 233.1 ± 71.4% (Fig. 4A). Consistently, VAS2870 also reduced O₂⁻ and H₂O₂ production in Aβ₁₋₄₀/thrombin-treated platelets to 257.4 ± 30.9% and 149.6 ± 13.0%, respectively (Fig. 4B, 4C), indicating that NOX is the primary source of ROS under these conditions. To determine whether NOX-derived ROS contribute to integrin αIIbβ3 signaling, we assessed integrin activation in the presence of VAS2870. Co-treatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin significantly increased integrin αIIb and β3 activation, which was markedly reduced by VAS2870 (135.3 ± 32.7% and 133.3 ± 22.3%, respectively; Fig. 5A, 5B). Moreover, VAS2870 pretreatment strongly attenuated platelet adhesion (181.5 ± 15.3%) and aggregation (1.7 ± 2.0%) induced by Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin (Fig. 5C, 5D). These findings demonstrate that NOX activity lies upstream of integrin αIIbβ3 and plays a central role in mediating Aβ₁₋₄₀-enhanced platelet adhesion and aggregation.

sec.title: Aβ₁₋₄₀ enhances platelet morphological activation and adhesion to hBMECs
sec.p: We further investigated whether Aβ₁₋₄₀ modulates platelet morphology and interaction with hBMECs, mimicking cerebrovascular conditions relevant to AD. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that thrombin-activated platelets exhibited elongated filopodia compared with controls. Pretreatment with Aβ₁₋₄₀ induced additional morphological alterations, including membrane blebbing, flattening, and fragmentation (Fig. 6A). These structural changes were markedly attenuated by pretreatment with VAS2870, Trolox, or eptifibatide, with platelets retaining a more typical discoid shape and reduced filopodia. To evaluate platelet–endothelial interactions, immunofluorescence microscopy was used to quantify platelet adhesion to hBMECs. In control samples, platelet adhesion was minimal; however, Aβ₁₋₄₀-potentiated thrombin treatment significantly increased platelet attachment to hBMECs (Fig. 6B). This effect was substantially suppressed by VAS2870, Trolox, and eptifibatide, suggesting that the combined action of Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin is mediated through ROS generation and integrin αIIbβ3 signaling, leading to platelet structural activation and increased cerebrovascular adhesion. These findings suggest that platelet-endothelial interactions could potentially contribute to AD-related vascular dysfunction.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study demonstrates that Aβ₁₋₄₀ enhances thrombin-induced platelet activation through a NOX-dependent increase in ROS production and integrin αIIbβ3 activation. Co-stimulation of platelets with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin resulted in enhanced ROS generation, integrin surface expression, cytoskeletal remodeling, and adhesion to brain microvascular endothelial cells, indicating that Aβ₁₋₄₀ potentiates thrombin-induced platelet activation. These effects were significantly attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of NOX, ROS scavenging, or integrin blockade, indicating a mechanistically integrated signaling pathway. These findings suggest that Aβ₁₋₄₀ primes platelets for enhanced responsiveness to subthreshold thrombin concentrations, thereby contributing to a prothrombotic and inflammatory vascular environment in AD.

Physiological hemostasis is maintained by the coordinated actions of endothelial cells, coagulation factors, and platelets, which together form localized clots at sites of vascular injury (McRae, 2011; Scridon, 2022). Upon activation by stimuli such as collagen, thromboxane A₂ (TXA₂), adenosine diphosphate (ADP), and thrombin, platelets adhere to damaged endothelium and aggregate to form hemostatic plugs (Tomaiuolo et al., 2017). These processes are tightly regulated under normal conditions to prevent either hemorrhage or pathological thrombosis (McRae, 2011). However, dysregulation of these pathways can result in pathological platelet activation, contributing to vascular dysfunction and thrombotic complications (Koupenova et al., 2017; Massberg et al., 2003). Recently, platelet hyperactivation has emerged as a pathological feature of AD, with accumulating evidence linking platelet dysfunction to neurovascular injury and cognitive decline. Circulating platelets from individuals with AD exhibit heightened reactivity and an increased propensity to form thrombi, a phenomenon correlated with elevated levels of Aβ peptides, particularly Aβ₁₋₄₀ (Stellos et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2018). Platelet-derived Aβ₁₋₄₀ co-localizes with thrombotic deposits, and higher plasma levels of Aβ₁₋₄₀ are associated with enhanced platelet aggregation in patients with AD (Gowert et al., 2014). These observations suggest that platelets may reflect systemic changes in AD and actively contribute to the progression of cerebrovascular pathology. Despite these findings, the mechanisms by which platelets participate in AD-associated vascular dysfunction remain poorly defined. In particular, how classical platelet agonists such as thrombin interact with circulating Aβ peptides to amplify platelet activation under early pathophysiological conditions has not been systematically addressed. It is important to clarify this relationship in order to understand how the vascular system contributes to AD.

Thrombin is a central effector of the coagulation cascade, functioning both as a hemostatic regulator and a potent proinflammatory mediator in vascular pathology. In patients with AD, high levels of prothrombin and thrombin have been found in the cerebral microvasculature and serum. This suggests that thrombin plays a role in the worsening of neurovascular dysfunction (Grammas et al., 2006; Gupta et al., 2005). Beyond its classical role in platelet activation, thrombin has been shown to increase endothelial permeability, promote neuroinflammation, and accelerate blood–brain barrier (BBB) breakdown (Park et al., 2023; Suo et al., 2004). These findings highlight thrombin’s broader contribution to cerebrovascular abnormalities in AD. Our data further support this role by demonstrating that Aβ₁₋₄₀ sensitizes platelets to subthreshold concentrations of thrombin. Pretreatment with low-dose Aβ₁₋₄₀ significantly enhanced platelet adhesion and aggregation in response to weak thrombin stimulation. This potentiating interaction is consistent with previous reports showing that nanomolar concentrations of Aβ₁₋₄₀ or Aβ₁₋₄₂ do not directly activate vascular cells but instead potentiate their responsiveness to secondary agonists such as ADP or collagen, or to vasoconstrictors (Paris et al., 2000; Shen et al., 2008). The ability of Aβ₁₋₄₀ to amplify thrombin responses may reflect a modulatory effect that is associated with increased platelet reactivity under conditions of low-grade vascular stress, which may plausibly occur in early AD. By recapitulating this pathophysiological state, our model provides a relevant platform for studying acute thromboinflammatory events that may initiate or accelerate neurodegenerative processes. Together, these findings support the existence of a thrombin–Aβ₁₋₄₀ interaction axis that contributes to vascular inflammation and platelet-driven pathology in AD, and suggest that early signaling events may play a decisive role in shaping subsequent platelet responses. Although NOX-derived ROS generation is sufficient to function as an initiating redox signal for platelet activation. Consistent with previous studies identifying NOX as a key intracellular signaling mediator in platelets, this early oxidative burst likely primes redox-sensitive pathways that culminate in sustained integrin αIIbβ3 activation and enhanced thrombin-mediated adhesion and aggregation (Chlopicki et al., 2004; Cipriano et al., 2023; Oh et al., 2025). In this context, NOX-ROS signaling acts as a trigger rather than a sustained effector, enabling transient oxidative events to produce prolonged functional consequences in platelet activation.

Building on this concept, our findings illuminate the intricate interplay between Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin in potentiating platelet activation via the NOX–ROS–integrin αIIbβ3 signaling axis—a pathway that appears to be a critical mediator of vascular pathology in AD. This axis represents a convergence point for amyloid-induced oxidative stress and thrombin-mediated platelet activation. While prior studies have independently implicated NOX-derived ROS in platelet activation induced by high concentrations of Aβ₁₋₄₀ (Lee et al., 2021) and in thrombin-driven thrombosis (Begonja et al., 2005), our results demonstrate, for the first time, that dual stimulation with Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin cooperatively activates this pathway, significantly amplifying platelet responses. NOX enzymes, particularly NOX2, are major sources of ROS in platelets and are essential for several key functions, including integrin αIIbβ3 activation, cytoskeletal remodeling, and granule secretion (Masselli et al., 2020; Nocella et al., 2023). In our study, pharmacological inhibition of NOX significantly reduced ROS production, suppressed surface expression of integrin αIIbβ3, and decreased platelet adhesion and aggregation. These findings emphasize the important function of NOX activity in promoting thrombosis rather than maintaining physiological hemostasis (Delaney et al., 2016). Consistent with this, inhibition of NOX reduced platelet aggregation in response to combined thrombin and Aβ₁₋₄₀ stimulation, supporting the concept that NOX activation plays a central role in thrombotic platelet activation in AD. Integrin αIIbβ3 functions in both inside-out and outside-in signaling. Inside-out signaling enhances the integrin’s affinity for ligands such as fibrinogen, while outside-in signaling, initiated upon ligand binding, promotes integrin clustering and further amplifies platelet activation (Begonja et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2019; Masselli et al., 2020; van den Kerkhof et al., 2021). Thrombin primarily induces inside-out signaling via protease-activated receptors (PAR1 and PAR4), whereas Aβ₁₋₄₀ has been shown to directly bind integrin αIIbβ3, triggering outside-in signaling (Donner et al., 2016, 2021; Nocella et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2021). This outside-in pathway involves signaling molecules such as Syk and PLCγ2, both of which are critical for ROS production and subsequent platelet activation (Donner et al., 2021). Our findings demonstrate that Aβ₁₋₄₀ significantly enhances thrombin-induced ROS generation in an integrin αIIbβ3-dependent manner, suggesting an augmented oxidative response under co-stimulation conditions. The observed increases in ROS levels and integrin αIIbβ3 activation support a mechanism in which Aβ₁₋₄₀ potentiates platelet activation via ROS-mediated outside-in signaling. It is well known that NOX2 is very important for thrombin-induced ROS production and integrin activation (Begonja et al., 2005; Vara et al., 2019). Here, we show that in the presence of Aβ₁₋₄₀, NOX inhibition effectively suppresses both ROS production and integrin αIIbβ3 activity, reinforcing the importance of NOX-mediated oxidative signaling in the heightened platelet reactivity associated with AD. Amplification of platelet activation through the NOX–ROS–integrin pathway is particularly relevant to AD-associated vascular pathology. Oxidative stress and Aβ₁₋₄₀-induced ROS contribute to neurovascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction (Canobbio et al., 2016), hallmarks of cerebrovascular injury in AD. Our research elucidates the mechanisms by which platelet activation may aggravate such injury. Morphological analysis by scanning electron microscopy revealed pronounced filopodia extension and membrane blebbing in response to Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin, features indicative of strong platelet–endothelium interactions and proinflammatory activation. Correspondingly, platelets exhibited significantly enhanced adhesion to cerebrovascular endothelial cells, an in vitro model recapitulating key features of the BBB. This pathological platelet–endothelial interaction may facilitate leukocyte recruitment, endothelial dysfunction, and BBB breakdown, key elements of vascular compromise in AD. Thus, the NOX–ROS–integrin signaling axis not only amplifies platelet activation but also contributes to cerebrovascular inflammation and barrier disruption, further linking platelet-driven thrombotic processes to the progression of neurodegenerative pathology.

These findings may have potential relevance. They raise the possibility that Aβ₁₋₄₀ is associated with vascular inflammatory processes and acts as a modulatory factor that enhances thrombin-induced platelet responses, which could contribute to increased thrombotic vulnerability in a disease already characterized by cerebrovascular fragility. Importantly, the attenuation of this enhanced response by NOX inhibition suggests that the NOX–ROS axis warrants further investigation as a potential therapeutic target. While these observations provide a mechanistic framework linking platelet activation to AD-associated vascular pathology, their translation significance should be interpreted with caution given the in vitro nature of the present study. Accordingly, pharmacological strategies aimed at limiting platelet activation or modulating oxidative stress may offer dual benefits by suppressing thromboinflammatory cascades and supporting the structural and functional integrity of the neurovascular unit in AD. Despite the strength of these results, it is important to consider some limitations. First, although the use of washed human platelets and hBMECs provides physiologically relevant insights, the data were derived from in vitro systems. Accordingly, in vivo validation is required, ideally in transgenic AD models or thrombotic injury models that replicate the systemic complexity of the disease. Second, while the present study focused on NOX enzymes, other sources of ROS, such as mitochondrial oxidases or xanthine oxidase, may also contribute to platelet activation and warrant investigation in future studies. Third, although thrombin signaling is known to be mediated by protease-activated receptors (PAR1 and PAR4), the specific receptor mechanisms underlying the combined effects of Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin remain to be elucidated. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that co-exposure to Aβ₁₋₄₀ and thrombin leads to enhanced platelet activation through a NOX–ROS–integrin αIIbβ3-dependent pathway. This mechanistic association between amyloidogenic stimuli, oxidative stress, and platelet-driven thrombogenic responses provides new insight into the vascular pathology of AD. Targeting key components of this signaling cascade may therefore represent a potential therapeutic approach for mitigating cerebrovascular injury and disease progression in AD.

caption.p: Aβ₁₋₄₀ enhances thrombin-induced platelet adhesion and aggregation. (A) Schematic overview of the experimental design and time points used for the indicated assays.
